answer:
For squared loss the negative gradient is y−current_prediction. Fit a regression tree to those residuals and add a learning-rate-scaled update. The included implementation uses depth-one trees, a valid GBDT special case, and begins at the mean target. Small learning rates typically need more stages. It does not implement XGBoost’s second-order objective, regularization, or histogram optimization.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** For squared loss, $F_m(x)=F_{m-1}(x)+\eta h_m(x)$ where $h_m$ fits residuals $y-F_{m-1}(x)$. Each new tree corrects current errors instead of independently predicting the target as in bagging. Depth, learning rate, and stage count jointly control fit; use validation-based stopping rather than relying on training residual decline. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02754)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://explained.ai/gradient-boosting/) and [2](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html#gradient-boosting).
